content:
Revelation 22:18 to 19 warns anyone who adds to or takes away from the words of the book. Some Christian writers read it as the closing seal on the whole Bible, so that no revelation can follow the New Testament. Some Muslim readers meet the argument when it is used against the Quran.

Five facts about the verse and the book show how far the argument can carry.

The text speaks of "this book", and the closing verses of Revelation give the warning.[1] A reader who takes the verse at its own words has a warning about the Apocalypse of John.

The wording belongs to a known form. The Torah carries a similar warning against adding to its commands, in Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32. Prophets and writings followed those verses, so the form did not close the scriptures at the time.

In the Greek church the Apocalypse was left out of the list at Laodicea, and of those of Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus and Amphilochius. Chrysostom never quotes it, according to Davidson.[2]

In the stichometry of Nicephorus, written between 806 and 815, it stands among the disputed books. The Syriac Peshito lacks it. A book that stands last in the Greek order and was doubted for centuries is a weak seal for the whole collection.

Davidson wrote that "The conception of canonicity and inspiration attaching to New Testament books did not exist till the time of Irenæus."[3] Irenaeus wrote in the later second century.

By that account no collection called the New Testament stood behind the warning when it was written. Davidson called a verse in 2 Peter that speaks of Paul's letters "the earliest example of the canonizing of any New Testament portion", and he dated it about 170.[4]

The councils of North Africa fixed the list of the West. The East doubted the Apocalypse for longer. Neither side based its list on the warning in Revelation.

The question of which books belong to the New Testament was settled in different regions by use, argument and local authority.

Many commentators read the verse as a protection for the text of that book against changes and false prophecy.[5] A reader can check that reading in a commentary.

A Muslim reader who meets the argument can answer it from the lists above. A warning inside one book of the Bible cannot close the collection that it joined many generations after it was written.

The bottom line

The warning at the end of Revelation guards one book. It does not close a Bible that the churches had not yet assembled, and it does not close a list that churches argued over for centuries.

Notes

  1. Revelation 22:18 to 19; Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32.
  2. Davidson, Canon, pp. 88 to 92 and 106; Davidson, Canon, p. 112, on the Greek order.
  3. Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (New York: Peter Eckler, 1877), p. 83.
  4. Davidson, Canon, p. 69, with the caution that his date for 2 Peter is later than most scholars give; Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987).
  5. David E. Aune, Revelation, 3 vols., Word Biblical Commentary (Dallas: Word Books, 1997 to 1998), on Revelation 22:18 to 19.
